processing: Fully oxidised black tea made by the CTC (crush, tear, curl) method, which cuts the leaf into small granules for a fast, strong infusion.
harvest_season: Not documented in detail for this factory. As is usual in equatorial East Africa, leaf comes in through much of the year from smallholder farms.
appearance_dry: Small, even, dark brown-black granules, as with other CTC teas.
appearance_liquor: Dark reddish-orange and dense, as is typical of CTC.
appearance_wet: A fine coppery-brown mass of small particles.
taste_profile: Published notes on this tea are thin. Typical black CTC from Rwanda is strong, brisk and malty, built to stand up to milk.

brewing.notes: Western style. Three minutes at most, because CTC turns harsh quickly; milk suits it.

vintage_note: Sold by grade and factory, largely in bulk, and not by year. As with other black CTC it is meant to be used fresh, ideally within a year or two of manufacture.
description:
Mulindi is a tea factory in Gicumbi District in northern Rwanda, described in reports as the country's oldest and largest by tea production. What makes it stand out is who owns it: since 2022 it has belonged entirely to the farmers who supply it.

The product is black CTC, which suits how Rwanda's industry works, as black tea makes up almost all of national output. The agriculture agency NAEB credits the factory with up to four million kg of made tea a year.

In the cup you can expect what is typical of Rwandan CTC rather than anything uniquely documented for Mulindi: a strong, brisk, malty brew. Keep the steep short and add milk if you like.

Mulindi mostly reaches drinkers inside blends, so a pack naming it is unusual. When buying, look for the grade and a production date; freshness matters more here than any year.
history:
Reports date the factory to 1960. In 2012 the government privatised it, and philanthropic investors, The Wood Foundation Africa and Gatsby Africa working through East Africa Tea Investments, took a 55% stake, with the remaining 45% held for farmers.

The handover completed in March 2022, leaving about 5,000 farmers in two cooperatives, COOPTHE and COOTHEVM, as full owners through Mulindi Tea Company. It was billed as Rwanda's first smallholder-owned tea factory.
